extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and readers interested in scientific misconduct and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the types of evidence, standards, and procedural considerations used to evaluate alleged research fraud in medical publications (as shown by a society investigation and external analyses). Focuses on criteria that trigger retractions, bans, or further scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of data manipulation and fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee found evidence of data manipulation and fraud in multiple publications; an editorial cited numerous publications where it was almost certain data manipulation and fraud had taken place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive signs of manipulated or falsified data (e.g., impossible values, altered datasets, inconsistencies between reported methods and results) are grounds for finding fraud and for institutional or society sanctions. The article cites a past review (Fujii case) where many papers were judged to contain falsified data (e.g., 172 of 212).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical improbability of random sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical analyses showing an extremely low likelihood that reported sampling was conducted randomly (e.g., Carlisle combined probabilities across trials and found p = 1.27 × 10⁻⁸).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical tests and probability assessments to detect anomalies in reported data; extremely small p-values indicating non-random sampling warrant further scrutiny and may indicate fabrication or manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition/duplication in figures (repeated lines across graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The repetition of lines in multiple graphs was noted as an indicator of questionable data (e.g., identical patterns appearing in separate figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect figures for duplicated lines, replicated patterns, or reused images/plots across supposedly independent experiments — these can be evidence of fabrication or inappropriate reuse of data.

rubrics_metrics.name: High number of retractions and association with known fraudulent authors
rubrics_metrics.description: A large count of retractions (Saitoh: 33 retractions; Fujii: record-breaking number, >180) and frequent co-authorship with a person known for falsified work were used as indicators of systemic problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of repeated retractions, especially clustered with the same co-authors, are red flags for broader misconduct and justify institutional investigation and potential sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe breaches of research ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee concluded that several publications contained severe breaches of research ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical breaches can include data fabrication/falsification, plagiarism, misleading reporting, failure to follow approved protocols, and are sufficient to justify retraction, professional discipline, or bans from societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to obtain proper patient consent
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one retraction occurred after a journal determined the authors had not obtained proper consent from patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of appropriate informed consent for patient data or participation is an independent ground for retraction and constitutes an ethical violation with legal and professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse influence on clinical care / patient safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The society stated that the individual had had an adverse influence on the provision of safe medical care, and thus lacked qualities required of an anaesthetist and researcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When research misconduct is likely to affect clinical practice or patient safety, institutions and professional societies may treat the misconduct as especially serious and pursue stronger disciplinary actions (e.g., permanent bans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/society procedural considerations (resignation vs. permanent ban)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual resigned when the investigation started; the society accepted the resignation under its regulations, but following the findings decided to permanently bar rejoining due to loss of credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules (articles of incorporation, membership regulations) may constrain immediate actions (e.g., accepting resignation), but findings of misconduct and reputational harm can nonetheless lead to permanent exclusion once established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and thoroughness of publication review
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee investigated approximately 40 publications by the individual and based conclusions on that review and related editorials and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive review of an individual's body of work (examining many publications) is a necessary step in investigations to determine patterns of misconduct rather than isolated errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of external analyses and editorial scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: External analyses (e.g., Carlisle's statistical review) and editorials in specialty journals contributed to identifying anomalies and motivating the society's investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent peer or statistical reviews, editorial commentary, and published critiques are important tools for detecting problems; journals and societies can rely on such external work to trigger formal inquiries.
